title: About Me
text:
Hello! I’m Matthew Diekmann, junior math major at Pomona College.
Welcome to my website!
This website was created for my Foundations of Data Science course and includes two data visualization projects using datasets from TidyTuesday.

title: About Me
text:
What you’ll find here
The Shark Tank tab has a text analysis of 415 Shark Tank pitches, attempting to discover trends for which types of products and pitches earn deals. The Data Viz menu contains two TidyTuesday analyses that use R to explore and visualize different datasets.

title: Billboard Hot 100 Number Ones
text:
For this analysis, I used the Billboard Hot 100 Number Ones dataset featured in TidyTuesday.
The dataset contains information about songs that reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100 between 1958 and January 2025. It includes information about the songs’ artists, genres, length, musical characteristics, and chart performance.
The original dataset was compiled by Chris Dalla Riva as part of his Billboard Hot 100 Number Ones Database.

title: Billboard Hot 100 Number Ones
text:
Load the Data


Code
library(tidyverse)

billboard <- readr::read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-08-26/billboard.csv"
)

topics <- readr::read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-08-26/topics.csv"
)

title: Billboard Hot 100 Number Ones
text:
Have Number-One Songs Gotten Shorter?
One question I was interested in was whether the length of number-one songs has changed over time. The dataset includes length_sec, which measures the length of each song in seconds. I converted this to minutes to make the visualization easier to interpret.


Code
billboard_length <- billboard |>
  mutate(
    year = as.integer(format(date, "%Y")),
    length_min = length_sec / 60
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(length_min))

ggplot(
  billboard_length,
  aes(x = year, y = length_min)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, method = "loess") +
  labs(
    title = "Length of Billboard Hot 100 Number-One Songs Over Time",
    subtitle = "Each point represents a song that reached number one",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Song length (minutes)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









The trend line makes it easier to see how the typical length of a number-one song has changed over time. Song lengths increased during parts of the late 20th century, but more recent number-one hits appear to have become shorter.

title: Billboard Hot 100 Number Ones
section: Which Genres Have the Most Number-One Hits?
text:
Which Genres Have the Most Number-One Hits?
I also wanted to see which genres appear most frequently among number-one songs. The variable cdr_genre gives the genre assigned to each song in the dataset.


Code
top_genres <- billboard |>
  filter(!is.na(cdr_genre)) |>
  count(cdr_genre, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

ggplot(
  top_genres,
  aes(
    x = reorder(cdr_genre, n),
    y = n
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Genres With the Most Billboard Hot 100 Number-One Songs",
    x = "Genre",
    y = "Number of number-one songs"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









This visualization shows which genres have accounted for the largest number of Billboard Hot 100 number-one songs in the dataset.

title: NCAA Men’s March Madness
text:
For this analysis, I used the NCAA Men’s March Madness dataset featured in TidyTuesday.
The data come from Nishaan Amin’s March Madness dataset and contain historical team tournament results along with public predictions for tournament teams.
The data cover men’s NCAA tournaments from 2008 through 2024, excluding 2020 because the tournament was canceled.

title: NCAA Men’s March Madness
text:
For this analysis, I used the NCAA Men’s March Madness dataset featured in TidyTuesday.
The data come from Nishaan Amin’s March Madness dataset and contain historical team tournament results along with public predictions for tournament teams.
The data cover men’s NCAA tournaments from 2008 through 2024, excluding 2020 because the tournament was canceled.

title: NCAA Men’s March Madness
text:
Load the Data


Code
library(tidyverse)

team_results <- readr::read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2024/2024-03-26/team-results.csv"
)

public_picks <- readr::read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2024/2024-03-26/public-picks.csv"
)

title: NCAA Men’s March Madness
section: Which Teams Have Made the Most Final Fours?
text:
Which Teams Have Made the Most Final Fours?
The F4 variable gives the number of times each program reached the Final Four. I looked at the teams with the most Final Four appearances in the dataset.


Code
top_final_four <- team_results |>
  filter(F4 > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(F4)) |>
  slice_head(n = 15)

ggplot(
  top_final_four,
  aes(
    x = reorder(TEAM, F4),
    y = F4
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Teams With the Most Final Four Appearances",
    subtitle = "NCAA men's tournament results in the TidyTuesday dataset",
    x = "Team",
    y = "Final Four appearances"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









This visualization shows which programs have reached the Final Four most often over the period represented in the dataset.

title: NCAA Men’s March Madness
section: Which Teams Did the Public Most Expect to Win in 2024?
text:
Which Teams Did the Public Most Expect to Win in 2024?
The public_picks dataset contains the percentage of public brackets that picked each team to advance through each round of the 2024 tournament. The FINALS variable gives the percentage of people who picked each team to win the championship.
I looked at the 10 teams with the highest championship pick percentages.


Code
top_public_picks <- public_picks |>
  mutate(
    finals_pct = readr::parse_number(FINALS)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(finals_pct)) |>
  arrange(desc(finals_pct)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

ggplot(
  top_public_picks,
  aes(
    x = reorder(TEAM, finals_pct),
    y = finals_pct
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Most Popular Public Picks to Win the 2024 Championship",
    subtitle = "Top 10 teams by percentage of public brackets",
    x = "Team",
    y = "Percent of public brackets picking team to win"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









Connecticut was the most popular public choice to win the championship in 2024, while several other highly rated teams also received substantial support. This visualization shows how concentrated public expectations were among the top contenders.
As a side note, UCONN went on to have one of the most dominant title runs in March Madness history, winning by a record average margin of 23 points per game.

title: What Gets a Deal on Shark Tank?
text:
I’ve always found Shark Tank interesting because entrepreneurs can walk into the room with completely different products, yet they’re all trying to accomplish the same thing: convince an investor to make a deal. Some businesses are built around complicated technology, while others are selling relatively simple everyday products.
For this project, I wanted to explore two questions:

Which product industries are most successful at securing deals?
Are certain words or types of language associated with higher deal rates?

I’m especially interested in the second question. Entrepreneurs often emphasize how their products solve problems, save time, or make life easier. I wanted to see whether those themes actually show up in the data.

title: What Gets a Deal on Shark Tank?
text:
I’ve always found Shark Tank interesting because entrepreneurs can walk into the room with completely different products, yet they’re all trying to accomplish the same thing: convince an investor to make a deal. Some businesses are built around complicated technology, while others are selling relatively simple everyday products.
For this project, I wanted to explore two questions:

Which product industries are most successful at securing deals?
Are certain words or types of language associated with higher deal rates?

I’m especially interested in the second question. Entrepreneurs often emphasize how their products solve problems, save time, or make life easier. I wanted to see whether those themes actually show up in the data.

title: What Gets a Deal on Shark Tank?
text:
The Data
I’m using a dataset of 415 pitches from Shark Tank, covering the show’s first six seasons. It contains 31 variables, including the startup’s name, product description, industry, and whether a deal was made.
For this analysis, the most important variables are:

title: Name of the startup
description: Written description of the product or business
category: Product industry
deal: Whether a deal was made

One important distinction is that these descriptions are not transcripts of the entrepreneurs’ actual pitches. I’m analyzing the language used to describe their products, rather than exactly what was said on television.
First, I wanted to get a general sense of the dataset.


Show code
shark_tank |>
  summarize(
    pitches = n(),
    industries = n_distinct(category, na.rm = TRUE),
    average_description_words = round(
      mean(str_count(description, "\\S+"), na.rm = TRUE),
      1
    ),
    overall_deal_rate = round(mean(deal, na.rm = TRUE) * 100, 1)
  )


# A tibble: 1 × 4
  pitches industries average_description_words overall_deal_rate
    <int>      <int>                     <dbl>             <dbl>
1     415         54                      36.3              51.6


There are 415 pitches across 54 product categories, with an overall deal rate of about 51.6%. The average product description contains roughly 36 words, giving us a reasonable amount of text to work with.

title: What Gets a Deal on Shark Tank?
section: 1. Which Industries Get the Most Deals?
text:
1. Which Industries Get the Most Deals?
My first question was whether certain types of businesses tend to perform better on Shark Tank.
I calculated the percentage of pitches receiving deals within each industry. One issue I ran into was that some categories had only one or two pitches, which could produce misleadingly high success rates.
To make the comparison more useful, I decided to focus on industries with at least 10 pitches.


Show code
industry_summary <- shark_tank |>
  filter(!is.na(category), !is.na(deal)) |>
  group_by(category) |>
  summarize(
    pitches = n(),
    deals = sum(deal),
    deal_rate = mean(deal) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(deal_rate))




Show code
industry_summary |>
  filter(pitches >= 10) |>
  mutate(
    category = fct_reorder(
      paste0(category, " (n=", pitches, ")"),
      deal_rate
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = category, y = deal_rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", width = 0.75) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 100),
    breaks = seq(0, 100, 20)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Shark Tank Deal Rates by Industry",
    subtitle = "Industries with at least 10 pitches",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Pitches Receiving a Deal (%)",
    caption = "Sample sizes shown in parentheses"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()










What stood out?
I was somewhat surprised by the results. Storage and Cleaning Products had the highest deal rate at 71.4%, with 10 of 14 pitches receiving deals. Baby and Child Care followed at 60.9%, while Specialty Food had a 58.2% deal rate across 55 pitches.
At the other end, Professional Services had a deal rate of only 20%, while Consumer Services came in at 25%.
One possible explanation is that tangible consumer products are easier for investors to understand, demonstrate, and imagine selling at scale. That’s just a hypothesis, though, and the data alone can’t confirm it.
It’s also worth remembering that even the categories included here have relatively small sample sizes. These differences are interesting, but they don’t necessarily mean one industry is inherently better than another.

title: What Gets a Deal on Shark Tank?
section: 2. Does Product Language Relate to Deal Success?
text:
2. Does Product Language Relate to Deal Success?
Next, I wanted to look beyond the industry categories and examine how the products themselves were described.
I decided to search for five general themes:

Technology: technology, software, app, digital, device
Health: health, fitness, medical, wellness
Convenience: easy, simple, convenient, portable
Innovation: innovative, unique, patented, new
Sustainability: sustainable, reusable, recycled, eco-friendly

Using str_detect() and regular expressions, I checked whether each description contained any of these words.


Show code
word_summary <- shark_tank |>
  filter(!is.na(description), !is.na(deal)) |>
  mutate(
    technology = str_detect(
      description,
      regex("\\b(technology|software|app|digital|device)\\b",
            ignore_case = TRUE)
    ),
    health = str_detect(
      description,
      regex("\\b(health|fitness|medical|wellness)\\b",
            ignore_case = TRUE)
    ),
    convenience = str_detect(
      description,
      regex("\\b(easy|simple|convenient|portable)\\b",
            ignore_case = TRUE)
    ),
    innovation = str_detect(
      description,
      regex("\\b(innovative|unique|patented|new)\\b",
            ignore_case = TRUE)
    ),
    sustainability = str_detect(
      description,
      regex("\\b(sustainable|reusable|recycled|eco-friendly)\\b",
            ignore_case = TRUE)
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      technology, health, convenience,
      innovation, sustainability
    ),
    names_to = "theme",
    values_to = "mentioned"
  ) |>
  filter(mentioned) |>
  group_by(theme) |>
  summarize(
    pitches = n(),
    deals = sum(deal),
    deal_rate = mean(deal) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(deal_rate))




Show code
word_summary |>
  mutate(
    theme = fct_reorder(
      paste0(str_to_title(theme), " (n=", pitches, ")"),
      deal_rate
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = theme, y = deal_rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", width = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = mean(shark_tank$deal, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "darkred"
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 100),
    breaks = seq(0, 100, 20)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Does Product Language Relate to Deal Success?",
    subtitle = "Dashed line represents the overall deal rate",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Pitches Receiving a Deal (%)",
    caption = "Themes can overlap; sample sizes shown in parentheses"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()










What stood out?
The biggest surprise was convenience-related language. Descriptions mentioning words like “easy,” “simple,” or “portable” had a 71.1% deal rate, substantially higher than the overall average of 51.6%.
Innovation-related language was associated with a 56.8% deal rate, while technology and health were both around 50%.
Sustainability-related descriptions actually had the lowest deal rate of the five themes, at 36.8%.
I found this interesting because I initially expected technology and innovation to perform especially well. Instead, the strongest association was with language suggesting that a product makes everyday life easier.
Of course, these themes overlap, and the wording may reflect the types of products being described rather than something that directly influences investment decisions.

title: What Gets a Deal on Shark Tank?
text:
3. A Closer Look at Convenience
Since convenience stood out so much, I wanted to explore it further.
First, I compared pitches that mentioned convenience-related words against pitches that didn’t.


Show code
convenience_comparison <- shark_tank |>
  filter(!is.na(description), !is.na(deal)) |>
  mutate(
    convenience = str_detect(
      description,
      regex(
        "\\b(easy|simple|convenient|portable)\\b",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      )
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(convenience) |>
  summarize(
    pitches = n(),
    deals = sum(deal),
    deal_rate = round(mean(deal) * 100, 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    convenience = if_else(
      convenience,
      "Convenience language",
      "No convenience language"
    )
  )

convenience_comparison |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Description Type", "Pitches",
      "Deals", "Deal Rate (%)"
    ),
    caption = "Deal outcomes by convenience-related language"
  )



Deal outcomes by convenience-related language

This comparison makes the difference even clearer. Pitches with convenience language received deals 71.1% of the time, compared with 49.6% for descriptions without those terms.
That’s a difference of 21.5 percentage points.
I wanted to see whether one particular word was responsible for this difference, so I separated the four convenience terms.


Show code
convenience_words <- shark_tank |>
  filter(!is.na(description), !is.na(deal)) |>
  mutate(
    easy = str_detect(
      description, regex("\\beasy\\b", ignore_case = TRUE)
    ),
    simple = str_detect(
      description, regex("\\bsimple\\b", ignore_case = TRUE)
    ),
    convenient = str_detect(
      description, regex("\\bconvenient\\b", ignore_case = TRUE)
    ),
    portable = str_detect(
      description, regex("\\bportable\\b", ignore_case = TRUE)
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(easy, simple, convenient, portable),
    names_to = "word",
    values_to = "mentioned"
  ) |>
  filter(mentioned) |>
  group_by(word) |>
  summarize(
    pitches = n(),
    deals = sum(deal),
    deal_rate = round(mean(deal) * 100, 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(deal_rate))

convenience_words |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Word", "Pitches", "Deals", "Deal Rate (%)"),
    caption = "Deal rates for individual convenience-related words"
  )

The results were especially interesting for “easy” and “simple.” Both appeared in descriptions with a 75% deal rate. “Easy” appeared in 20 pitches, while “simple” appeared in 12.
“Convenient” technically had a 100% deal rate, but it only appeared twice, so I wouldn’t read much into that result. “Portable” had a 40% deal rate across five pitches.
Overall, the findings suggest that products described as easy or simple may be worth investigating further, although the samples are too small to make strong predictions.

Looking at actual startup descriptions
I also wanted to see some specific examples instead of relying entirely on averages.
For this part, I used str_extract() to identify the first convenience-related word in each description, along with str_count() to measure description length.
I used a regular expression with negative lookbehind and lookahead:

(?<![a-z]) ensures the match is not immediately preceded by a letter.
(?![a-z]) ensures the match is not immediately followed by a letter.

These prevent the expression from accidentally matching parts of longer words.


Show code
convenience_examples <- shark_tank |>
  filter(!is.na(description)) |>
  mutate(
    word_count = str_count(description, "\\S+"),
    convenience_word = str_extract(
      str_to_lower(description),
      "(?<![a-z])(easy|simple|convenient|portable)(?![a-z])"
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(convenience_word)) |>
  select(title, category, convenience_word, word_count, deal)

convenience_examples |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Startup", "Industry", "Convenience Word",
      "Description Words", "Deal"
    ),
    caption = "Examples of startups using convenience-related language"

title: What Gets a Deal on Shark Tank?
section: 4. Is Convenience Language More Common in Certain Industries?
text:
4. Is Convenience Language More Common in Certain Industries?
One possible explanation for the convenience finding is that these words might simply appear more frequently in industries that already have high deal rates.
To explore this, I calculated how frequently convenience-related language appeared within each industry.


Show code
industry_language <- shark_tank |>
  filter(!is.na(description), !is.na(category), !is.na(deal)) |>
  mutate(
    convenience = str_detect(
      description,
      regex(
        "\\b(easy|simple|convenient|portable)\\b",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      )
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(category) |>
  summarize(
    pitches = n(),
    convenience_pitches = sum(convenience),
    convenience_pct = round(mean(convenience) * 100, 1),
    deal_rate = round(mean(deal) * 100, 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(pitches >= 10) |>
  arrange(desc(convenience_pct))

industry_language |>
  select(category, pitches, convenience_pct, deal_rate) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(

Interestingly, the industries that mentioned convenience most frequently weren’t necessarily the ones with the highest deal rates.
Toys and Games had the highest proportion of convenience-related descriptions at 25%, but its overall deal rate was only 43.8%. Meanwhile, Storage and Cleaning Products had the highest deal rate among the industries we examined, despite convenience language appearing in only 7.1% of its descriptions.
This suggests that the relationship between convenience language and deal success isn’t simply explained by the highest-performing industries using those words more often.
However, this table doesn’t establish whether the relationship holds within individual industries. There aren’t enough convenience-related pitches in many categories to make reliable comparisons.

title: What Gets a Deal on Shark Tank?
text:
Conclusion
Going into this project, I expected that businesses involving technology or innovative products might have the highest success rates on Shark Tank. Instead, I found that relatively practical industries, such as Storage and Cleaning Products, performed particularly well in this dataset.
The most interesting result to me was the relationship between convenience-related language and deal outcomes. Descriptions mentioning words like “easy” or “simple” were associated with noticeably higher deal rates than descriptions without those terms.
One possible interpretation is that investors value products that solve clear, everyday problems. However, this is only a possible explanation, not something the analysis proves.
There are several limitations to keep in mind. The dataset covers only the first six seasons, the industry samples are sometimes small, and the product descriptions aren’t necessarily the actual words used by entrepreneurs during their pitches. Additionally, factors like valuation, sales, profitability, and the entrepreneurs themselves likely play major roles in investment decisions.
Ultimately, I think the most interesting takeaway is that a complicated or innovative product isn’t necessarily more attractive to investors than a simple one. Sometimes the appeal of a business might come from how clearly it solves a problem. With a little extra research, I found that this idea is reflected among Shark Tank’s all-time most succesful products. We see simple, effective items such as Scrub Daddy, Bombas socks, and DUDE Wipes.

title: What Gets a Deal on Shark Tank?
text:
Data Source
The dataset comes from the public GitHub repository AlfonsoCabello/SharkTank, specifically the shark_tank.csv file.
The repository contains structured information about pitches from the first six seasons of the television show Shark Tank, including startup descriptions, product categories, deal outcomes, and investment details.
